Aitareya Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The उपनिषद्स् which usually form the last part of the वेदस् and hence known as Vedānta (anta = end) contain the quintessence of Hindu philosophy. They deal with certain fundamental questions of metaphysics: the Creator, process of च्रेअतिओन्, nature of the created world, true and apparent nature of the individual, relationship between this individual and the Creator, goal of life and the path that helps achieving it.
Out of the ten or twelve उपनिषद्स् considered more ancient and important the Aitareya Upaniṣad is also one. It forms part of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (adhyāyas 4 to 6 of the 2nd Āraṇyaka) of the Ṛgveda. Mahidāsa ऐतरेय who is mentioned in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.16.7) is the ṛṣi to whom this Upaniṣad was revealed.
The previous parts of the Āraṇyaka contain instructions regarding कर्म (Vedic rituals) and prāṇopāsanā (meditation on प्राण, the vital breath or energy). Anyone who has performed these two seriously and sincerely will become fit for आत्मज्ञान (self-knowledge). This has been expounded in the next three (4 to 6) adhyāyas which comprise this Upaniṣad.
The Upaniṣad starts with a description of च्रेअतिओन्. In the beginning the आत्मन् alone existed. He reflected: ‘Let me create the worlds.’ Then he created four worlds: ambholoka (supercelestial region of waters), marīciloka (the heavens with their celestial lights), maraloka (the mortal earth) and āpoloka (the subterranean region of waters). Desiring to create the protectors for these worlds, he proceeded to create first, Virāṭpuruṣa (‘World-Person’)—an intermediate entity subsisting between the आत्मन् and the universe—whom he fashioned out of the waters. From him proceeded the organs of senses, then their corresponding functions and lastly the deities or cosmic powers corresponding to such functions in the cosmos.
The आत्मन् who can now be called ईश्वर, made the Virāṭpuruṣa subject to hunger and thirst. Consequently the deities born out of him also became subject to the same limitation. On the request from the deities for a suitable locus from which they can act, he created the human body into which they gladly entered. Hunger and thirst which were left behind were also provided a place, but as an integral part of these deities.
On further reflection, realizing the need for ‘food’ by the Virāṭpuruṣa along with the deities, ईश्वर created ड़ोओद् articles like corn and animals. The Virāṭ-पुरुष was able to grasp this ड़ोओद् only with the apānavāyu (the prāṇic energy responsible for digestion and excretion) and not with the other deities (or इन्द्रियस्, i.e., faculties).
Since the body of the Virāṭpuruṣa could not live without the presence of the आत्मन् or ईश्वर, he entered into it through the ब्रह्मरन्ध्र (the aperture in the crown of the head).
The Upaniṣad then describes how the jīvātman (the आत्मन् bound in the body) transmigrates, conception, birth and rebirth being his three kinds of births. It also quotes the great sage वामदेव who realised his true nature as the आत्मन्, free from the shackles of bodies and senses, even while he was in the womb of his मोथेर्.
The last section describes आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन् as ‘prajñāna’ (consciousness) because of whose presence only all experience is possible. One of the four famous mahāvākyas (great dicta) of the Upaniṣadic literature viz., prajñānaṁ brahma (‘Prajñāna is ब्रह्मन्’) comes in this section (

).
Out of the several theories of च्रेअतिओन् given in the उपनिषद्स्, the one given here appears to be more enigmatic if not altogether inscrutable. However, a little reflection is enough to convince that it falls in line with the general philosophy of the उपनिषद्स्. The various accounts of च्रेअतिओन् given in the उपनिषद्स् normally fall into three categories: through त्रिवृत्करण (triplication) as in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad; through पञ्चीकरण (quin-tuplication) as in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad; and through the Virāṭpuruṣa (cosmic person) as here.
The purpose of च्रेअतिओन् is to give the unredeemed jīvas (individual souls) one more chance for redemption. This means that each of the jīvas must have a suitable body and a sphere of activity. The latter is provided by the various lokas or worlds, states of being, and the Virāṭpuruṣa forms the matrix as it were from which the former is shaped. Apart from the physical body, the sense-organs and the मिन्द्, located in it, form the basis of all activity. Hence their च्रेअतिओन् has also been des-cribed. The deities like अग्नि and आदित्य mentioned here are the लोकपालस्, ‘protectors of the worlds’. They are the entities endowed with the power of maintaining order in the created worlds. At the cosmic level, each of them represents the totality or essence of that particular power manifested in च्रेअतिओन्. At the individual level, it is the controlling power of the particular faculty. For instance, अग्नि at the cosmic level represents the fire-principle, whereas the same at the level of the individual body represents the power of speech which illumines the dark areas of unknown fields of knowledge.
The ‘hunger and thirst’ of the deities is a sign of their incompleteness and hence indicates that they too have fallen into the ocean of सṁसार (transmigratory existence). This is but natural since the whole of the created world, starting with the Virāṭpuruṣa himself, is within the realm of सṁसार. Their ‘food’ is the corresponding object of sense, united with which, the deities feel satisfied.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Aitareya Āraṇyaka
------------------------------------------
Each of the four वेदस्, the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, is again divided into four parts: Saṁhitā, ब्राह्मण, Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad.
The Aitareya Āraṇyaka (2500 B. C.) is one of the two आरण्यकस् belonging to the Ṛgveda, the other being Śāṅkhāyana Āraṇyaka. It has five main divisions each of which is also given the appellation ‘āraṇyaka.’ For instance, the first division is called ‘prathamāraṇyaka,’ the second ‘dvitīyāraṇyaka’ and so on. The total number of adhyāyas or chapters is eighteen. These adhyāyas are again subdivided into khaṇḍas or small sections.
The first āraṇyaka describes the ‘mahāvrata’ which is a part of the Sattra-याग known as ‘Gavāmayana’ and performed on the penultimate day. (See SATTRAYĀGA and GAVĀMAYANA for details.) This rite derives its name primarily from the fact that a सामन् (a hymn from the Sāmaveda) called ‘mahāvrata’ is sung while offering a cup of सोम juice to प्रजापति (‘Father of beings’) who is also called ‘mahān’ (‘the great one’). A priest playing on a harp and another sitting on a swing, shooting of arrows, mimetic fights, dancing with water pitchers on the head by the servants—these are some of the important side-lights of the ritual.
The first three adhyāyas of the second āraṇyaka deal with uktha or niṣkevalya शस्त्र, and describe प्राण, the vital force and the greatness of पुरुष (human being). Niṣkevalya शस्त्र consists of certain Ṛgvedic stanzas which are to be chanted (and not sung) at the time of pressing the सोम juice during sacrifices like गवामयन. Certain meditations connected with it are described.
The rest of this āraṇyaka (i.e., the fourth, fifth and sixth adhyāyas) comprises the well-known Aitareya Upaniṣad. (For details see AITAREYA UPANIṢAD.)
The third āraṇyaka deals with the special upāsanās or contemplations and their fruits connected with the saṁhitā-pāṭha, पदपाठ and क्रमपाठ (the vedic texts and their systematic breaking up for convenience in remembering and interpreting). It also deals with the ariṣṭas (ill-omens) manifesting through certain physical signs like seeing the sun as मोओन्, as not seeing one’s head through the mirror or through द्रेअम्स्, as seeing a man of black complexion—all of which forebode death. Names of certain ancient ṛṣis like शाकल्य, Māṇḍūkeya, Pāñcālacaṇḍa and तार्क्ष्य are mentioned as the propagators of the upāsanas.
The fourth āraṇyaka which is very short deals with the महानाम्नी mantras of Sāmaveda which are to be chanted on the fifth day of the महाव्रत.
The fifth āraṇyaka which is the last, deals with many ritualistic details of the महाव्रत.
Hindu tradition ascribes only the first three आरण्यकस् to ऐतरेय, the fourth and the fifth being attributed to आश्वलायन and his गुरु शौनक.

Aitareya Brāhmaṇa
------------------------------------------
The ब्राह्मण is the second important section of the वेदस्, the first being the Saṁhitā. Whereas the Saṁhitā is in poetry and deals with a variety of subjects, the ब्राह्मण, which is in prose, confines itself to liturgy, describing the modus operandi of the various sacrifices.
The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (3000-2500 B. C.) is the longer one of the two extant ब्राह्मणस् of the Ṛgveda—the other being Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa—and is attributed to Mahidāsa ऐतरेय (See AITAREYA for details.). There is reason to believe that this is, perhaps, an abridged edition of an earlier and much bigger work. The book is divided into eight pañcikās (quintets) each consisting of five adhyāyas or chapters which are again subdivided into kaṇḍikās or short sections. In all, there are 285 kaṇḍikās spread over 40 adhyāyas. The language is almost as archaic as that of the Saṁhitā and certain word-groups tend to appear repeatedly.
Since this work contains many details of sacrificial rites which are rather bewildering to the modern मिन्द्, only a very brief summary of the contents will be attempted here. The first thirteen adhyāyas give a minute description of the various duties and responsibilities of the होतृ (principal priest of the Ṛgveda) (See HOTṚ for details.) in the sacrifice called अग्निष्टोम. अग्निष्टोम being a प्रकृति or prototype of all other Somayāgas (which are its vikṛtis or modifications or versions) it has been given the pride of place here. Adhyāyas 15-17 describe the sacrifices Ukthya, अतिरात्र and षोडशी which are all vikṛtis of अग्निष्टोम. The 18th adhyāya deals with the Sattrayāgas (which take a full year to perform) and the part the होतृ is expected to play in it. The next six adhyāyas (19 to 24) concern themselves with the sacrifice called द्वादशाह, the emphasis again being on the instructions to the hotṛs. अग्निहोत्र is described in the 25th. The duties of the होतृ and his assistants in the Somayāgas which take several weeks are described in the five adhyāyas 26 to 30. The last two pañcikās comprising adhyāyas 31 to 40, contain interesting material from which plenty of information can be gathered on contempo-rary history. राजसूय sacrifice is the main theme of the adhyāyas 31-35. It is here that we come across the well-known story of शुनश्शेफ and हरिश्चन्द्र. The last section (adhyayās 36 to 40) deals with the चोरोनतिओन् of इन्द्र and gives a long list of the various kings who were coronated by ṛṣis following the same pattern of इन्द्र’s चोरोनतिओन्. The work ends with the exhortation to the king to appoint a पुरोहित (priest) and the qualifications the latter has to possess to deserve the honour.
Some of the special features of this ब्राह्मण may now be noted: It appears that the deity विष्णु was highly respected by the Vedic society of that time. A number of earlier religious works are quoted from which we can surmise the existence of other ब्राह्मण works which are not available now. It is interesting to note that the work criticises the views of other works and earlier teachers, if and when found necessary.
Out of the several ṛks (Ṛgvedic mantras) quoted here, a few have not been found in the extant Ṛgveda Saṁhitā. Perhaps another śākhā or branch of the Ṛgveda Saṁhitā different from the Śākala recension available now, must have existed.
The whole text is overwhelmingly weighed in favour of the sacrificial system of religion leaving practically no room for metaphysical ideas as, for instance, in the उपनिषद्स्.
By the time of this ब्राह्मण, Āryan culture had already spread to Eastern India, though Central India continued to be the heart of it. Kings of the कुरु-Pāñcāla race were ruling in Central India. Kings of the east were called ‘sāmrāṭ’ and of the south ‘bhoja.’ Emperors who conquered these used to assume titles like ‘ekarāṭ,’ ‘sārvabhauma’ or ‘parameṣṭhin.’ They believed that the rite ‘mahābhiṣeka’ (by which इन्द्र was coronated) would induce in the king the necessary power and inspiration to achieve this sovereignty.
Emperors and kings were fond of performing long and complicated sacrifices, especially the ‘mahābhiṣeka.’ Curds, honey, ghee and water were being used in this rite for anointing and sprinkling. Though the State exercised full control over the people, the ब्राह्मणस् were deemed to have transcended it.
The book contains a list of twelve kings who underwent this महाभिषेक rite. जनमेजय, the great-grandson of अर्जुन as also भरत, the son of दुष्यन्त and शकुन्तला are included in this list.
Though the people were ardently devoted to the sacrificial rites they had not neglected the life here and now. ब्राह्मणस् vied with one another to exhibit their erudition while the kṣattriyas did the same in the field of physical prowess and skill in arms.
See also BRĀHMAṆAS and MAHĀBHI-ṢEKA.

Aitareya
(‘son of इतरा’)
------------------------------------------
Aitareya, also known as Mahidāsa ऐतरेय, is the ṛṣi (sage) credited with the authorship of the ब्राह्मण, Āraṇyaka and Upaniṣad (of the Ṛgveda) that go in his name. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3.16.7) mentions him as having lived for 116 years as a result of meditating upon his life as a यज्ञ or sacrifice. This has become known as ‘puruṣayajña.’
According to other accounts given in the पुराणस्, he was the son of इतरा and Māṇḍuki (whence his name ऐतरेय). Since he never spoke, the मोथेर् इतरा, thinking that he was dumb, prayed to Mahī (mother Earth) who blessed him with divine knowledge and wisdom (whence the additional appellation Mahīdāsa or Mahidāsa).
He was an ardent devotee of Lord वासुदेव and had been repeating constantly the dvādaśākṣarī mantra (the twelve-lettered मन्त्र, viz., ‘Oṁ namo bhagavate Vāsudevāya’). Once the Deity appeared to him in a vision and comman-ded him to take to the second stage of life, that of the householder, to please his parents. Accordingly he went to one Harimedhas who was performing a sacrifice, exhibited his divine powers and knowledge and secured the hand of his daughter in मर्रिअगे as also enough wealth.
The Vedic sections associated with his name are said to have been revealed to him in the yajñaśālā (sacrificial shed) of Harimedhas.
